المتحدة، جينيفر لوسيتا، خلال اجتماع مجلس الأمن الهجوم الذي وقع في 24 أغسطس وأسفر عن مقتل ثلاثة جنود من قوات حفظ السلام، مؤكدةً ضرورة محاسبة المتورطين. كما انتقدت لوسيتا الحكومة في جنوب السودان لتجاوزاتها المتعلقة بعرقلة الدوريات، وتأخير الموافقات، ومضايقة موظفي الأمم المتحدة، مشددةً على أن هذه الممارسات تعرض حياة المدنيين للخطر. ودعت قادة جنوب السودان إلى إنهاء الأعمال القتالية واستئناف الحوار السياسي، مع التأكيد على أهمية إعطاء بعثة “يونميس” حرية الحركة للقيام بمسؤولياتها في حماية المدنيين. وحذرت من أن استمرار عراقيل عمل البعثة وتصاعد العنف قد يؤثران سلباً على القرارات الأمريكية المستقبلية بشأن المساعدات والدبلوماسية ومستقبل بعثة الأمم المتحدة في البلاد. وكانت واشنطن قد أكدت في السابق على ضرورة رفع القيود المفروضة على عمليات “يونميس”، مشيرةً إلى أن عدم التعاون سيهدد قدرة البعثة على أداء مهامها. السودان المتحدة بعثة جنوب قوات الخبر السابق المتحف القومي للحضارة يطلق النسخة الثانية من «أسبوع الفن الإسلامي» في 22 نوفمبر الخبر التالي غرفة السياحة تعلن تجاوز 400 ألف مصري أداء العمرة منذ يوليو الماضي اقرأ أيضاً تحذيرات من مجموعة الأزمات الدولية بشأن خطر عودة جنوب السودان إلى صراع شامل منذ 12 دقيقة مصادر تُفيد بإطلاق صاروخ باليستي نحو مأرب من موقعين في محافظة ذمار اليمنية منذ 24 دقيقة نائب رئيس مجلس النواب العراقي يؤكد العمل على تحديث التشريعات الاقتصادية وتقديم تسهيلات لجذب الاستثمارات منذ 36 دقيقة الاستاد الإخباري موقع إخباري مستقل يقدّم الخبر لحظة بلحظة بدقة وحياد، ويغطي الشأن المحلي والعربي والدولي والاقتصاد والثقافة والمنوعات. الأقسام أخبار مصر أخبار دوليّة أخبار السعودية منوعات أخبار التعليم العلوم والتكنولوجيا ترددات عن الموقع الرئيسية اتصل بنا من نحن بحث مع المدير التنفيذي لبرنامج الأغذية العالمي سبل تعزيز التعاون المشترك و الخرطوم 10 نوفمبر 2026 – نقلت الحكومة السودانية للأمم المتحدة اعتراضها مجدداً على التحليلات المتعلقة بالأمن الغذائي دون أن تكون طرفاً في إعدادها. وفي مطلع نوفمبر الجاري كشفت منظمة الأمم المتحدة لرعاية الطفولة “يونيسف” ومجموعة التغذية، عن تجاوز السودان عتبة الطوارئ التي حددتها منظمة الصحة العالمية عند 15% في 49% من مسوحات التغذية التي أُجريت في السودان خلال عام 2026. ويحتاج 8.4 ملايين سوداني إلى مساعدات التغذية خلال هذا العام، منهم 4.19 ملايين شخص يُتوقع أن يعانوا من سوء التغذية الحاد، من بينهم 824,827 طفلاً، بحسب الأمم المتحدة. لكن الحكومة السودانية ترفض الاعتراف بوجود أزمة غذاء في البلاد. وقالت يونيسف ومجموعة التغذية، في تقرير يغطي الفترة من يناير إلى سبتمبر، إن “18 من أصل 37 مسحاً تغذوياً، بما يعادل 49% من المسوحات، أظهرت انتشاراً لسوء التغذية الحاد عند عتبة الطوارئ، فيما سجلت 7 مسوحات نسباً تبلغ 20% أو أكثر”. وبدأ المدير التنفيذي لبرنامج الأغذية العالمي لوك ليندبيرج، الثلاثاء، سلسلة اجتماعات مع المسؤولين في الحكومة السودانية شملت رئيس الوزراء ووزيري الزراعة والخارجية. وقالت وزارة الزراعة والري السودانية، في بيان صحفي، إن الوزير عصمت قرشي، بحث مع ليندبيرج سبل تعزيز التعاون المشترك وتطوير التدخلات الداعمة للقطاع الزراعي والأمن الغذائي في السودان. وأوضح أن القطاع الزراعي يمضي في مسار التعافي، وأن المزارعين يواصلون الإنتاج رغم ظروف الحرب والتحديات المناخية، مشيراً إلى أن المساحات المزروعة خلال الموسم الحالي تجاوزت 10 ملايين هكتار، بما يعكس قدرة القطاع على الصمود ومواصلة الإنتاج. وأشار الوزير إلى وجود مناطق تعاني من الهشاشة، خاصة التي تسيطر عليها المليشيات المتمردة، وتواجه أوضاعاً إنسانية وإنتاجية صعبة، واصفاً ما يحدث فيها بأنه عمليات تجويع، ومشدداً على ضرورة توجيه التدخلات الإنسانية والتنموية وفق الاحتياجات الفعلية للمجتمعات والمزارعين. وفيما يتعلق بالتصنيف المرحلي المتكامل للأمن الغذائي (IPC)، “جدد قرشي رفض الحكومة إجراء أو نشر أي تحليلات بشأن الأمن الغذائي في السودان دون مشاركتها”. وشدد على ضرورة احترام السيادة السودانية وضمان مشاركة المؤسسات الحكومية المختصة في جمع البيانات والتحقق منها وتحليلها، مؤكداً انفتاح الحكومة على استكشاف آليات جديدة لتحليل الأمن الغذائي والتغذوي، بما يضمن المهنية والشفافية ودقة المعلومات. ويُعد التصنيف المرحلي المتكامل للأمن الغذائي (IPC) الذي انسحبت منه الحكومة في أواخر ديسمبر 2024 أداة دولية مشتركة لتحليل وتصنيف شدة انعدام الأمن الغذائي وسوء التغذية، استناداً إلى أدلة علمية ومعايير موحدة، ويقسم الأوضاع إلى خمس مراحل، تبدأ من المرحلة الأولى التي تعبر عن انعدام الأمن الغذائي الحاد أو الظروف الطبيعية، وصولاً إلى المرحلة الخامسة التي تمثل المجاعة أو الكارثة الإنسانية. من جانبه، أكد المدير التنفيذي لبرنامج الأغذية العالمي استمرارهم في تقديم المساعدات الإنسانية وتعزيز الشراكات لمواجهة التحديات، لافتاً إلى أن نحو 266 مليون شخص حول العالم يواجهون مستويات حادة من انعدام الأمن الغذائي، وأن النزاعات تمثل أحد أبرز أسباب تفاقم هذه الأوضاع. وكشف عن تمكن البرنامج من الوصول إلى نحو 600 ألف سوداني وتقديم المساعدات لهم، مؤكداً أن تعزيز الشراكة والتعاون مع الحكومة السودانية يمثل عاملاً أساسياً لضمان نجاح البرامج وتحقيق أثر أكبر على أرض الواقع. وكان رئيس الوزراء كامل إدريس قد التقى أيضاً المدير التنفيذي لبرنامج الأغذية العالمي، لوك ليندبرج، الذي أعرب في تصريح صحفي عن شكره لحكومة السودان على حُسن الاستقبال خلال زيارته الأولى للبلاد بصفته مديراً تنفيذياً للبرنامج، موضحاً أنه عقد خلال الزيارة اجتماعات وصفها بالمثمرة مع وزير الخارجية، ووزير الزراعة والري. الكلمات: الأمن الغذائي التصنيف المرحلي المتكامل الخرطوم السودان السودان تحت نيران المسيّرات.. قتلى في دارفور وهجمات على منشآت حيوية وأضاف أن سكان السودان "يتحدثون عن 3 أمور: الأمان والتعليم والمياه، والطائرات المسيّرة المسلحة تسلبهم هذه الأمور الثلاثة". وقد أسفرت الحرب الدائرة منذ أبريل/نيسان 2023 بين قوات الدعم السريع والجيش السوداني عن مقتل أكثر من 200 ألف شخص، بحسب تقديرات العاملين في المجال الإنساني، وتسببت في أكبر أزمة جوع ونزوح في العالم. ويعتمد طرفا النزاع بشكل متزايد على الضربات البعيدة المدى بمسيّرات قادرة على التحليق لمئات الكيلومترات. وقُتل أكثر من 1100 شخص في هجمات بطائرات مسيّرة في أنحاء السودان خلال النصف الأول من العام الجاري، وفق الأمم المتحدة. تفاقم الأزمة الإنسانية وأوضح إلدر أن تزايد استخدام الطائرات المسيّرة لاستهداف البنية التحتية المدنية يفاقم أيضا تداعيات موجة الجفاف التي تضرب السودان، وحذّر من أن "الطائرات المسيّرة والجفاف يطبقان على أطفال السودان من كل جانب". وفي تشرين الأول/أكتوبر وحده، تعرضت محطات توليد الكهرباء في مختلف أنحاء البلاد لما لا يقل عن 15 ضربة بطائرات مسيّرة، وفق إلدر. إقرأ أيضاً سياسة - السودان حرب المسيّرات في السودان.. لماذا تتصاعد الهجمات على محطات الكهرباء؟ وأوضح أن استهداف محطات الطاقة يؤدي الى "توقف مضخات المياه وتعطل عمليات معالجة المياه، ما يرغم العائلات على اللجوء إلى بدائل باهظة التكلفة وغير آمنة"، ما يعرض السكان لخطر الإصابة بأمراض تنتقل عبر المياه، مثل الكوليرا. ومن المتوقع أن يعاني نحو 825 ألف طفل دون الخامسة من أشد أشكال سوء التغذية فتكا هذه السنة، وفق إلدر. وحذّرت المفوضية السامية للأمم المتحدة لشؤون اللاجئين والمنظمة الدولية للهجرة، الجمعة، من خطر فقدان ملايين النازحين بسبب الحرب في السودان للمأوى الطارئ، في ظل استنزاف مخزون المساعدات الإنسانية جراء نقص التمويل. وأوضحت الوكالتان الأمميتان أن نحو 15.4 مليون شخص في السودان يحتاجون إلى إيواء عاجل ومستلزمات معيشية أساسية، إلا أن القيود المالية الراهنة تحول دون تقديم المساعدات إلا لنحو 10% فقط من إجمالي المحتاجين. تابع القراءة المصادر أ ف ب تابع آخر أخبار التلفزيون العربي عبر Google News الدلالات النزاع العسكري في السودان الجيش السوداني قوات الدعم السريع اليونيسف الطفولة النزوح تغطية خاصة المشهد السوداني المزيد من السودان مطلوب للجنائية الدولية.. الجيش السوداني يعتقل أحمد هارون القمر الصناعي والسودنة.. تاريخ السودان في أسماء تياب النساء الجيش السوداني يعلن إسقاط مسيّرة "معادية" في ولاية غرب كردفان موضوعات ذات صلة سياسة - العالم العربي معارك على محاور عدة في السودان.. ماذا يجري في النيل الأزرق؟ سياسة - العالم العربي تصاعد المواجهات في كردفان والنيل الأزرق.. قتلى بهجوم على محطة وقود سياسة - العالم العربي حرب السودان.. انشقاق جديد عن الدعم السريع وتصاعد معارك النيل الأزرق سياسة - العالم العربي منشآت الطاقة هدف للمسيّرات.. قصف يطال محطة "أبو حمد" في السودان تغطيّة إخبارية شاملة ومتعدّدة الوسائط للأحداث العربيّة والعالمية، ويتيح الوصول إلى شبكة منوّعة من البرامج السياسية والاجتماعية. روابط العربي سياسة اقتصاد فن وثقافة رياضة منوعات وثائقيات العربي بالصور البث المباشر برامج عن العربي ترددات البث اقتراح برامج من نحن أعلن معنا وظائف اتفاقية استخدام الموقع حقوق الملكية الفكرية فريق تحرير الموقع فريق عمل القناة راديو التلفزيون العربي اتصل بنا instagram twitter facebook YouTube telegram whatsapp جميع الحقوق محفوظة © التلفزيون العربي 2026

sudan.summary: حذرت مجموعة الأزمات الدولية من خطر عودة جنوب السودان إلى صراع واسع النطاق، مشيرة إلى تراجع تنفيذ اتفاق السلام لعام 2018 وتزايد الانقسامات السياسية قبل الانتخابات المقررة في 22 ديسمبر. جاء هذا التحذير على لسان مدير برنامج إفريقيا في المجموعة، موريثي موتيجا، خلال جلسة لمجلس الأمن. وأكد أن احتجاز النائب الأول السابق للرئيس رياك مشار واستبدال نواب من المعارضة يمثلان انتكاسات كبيرة لمسار السلام. كما أشار إلى أن نحو 10 ملايين شخص يحتاجون إلى مساعدات إنسانية، بينما يعاني 7.8 مليون شخص من مستويات حادة من الجوع. وازدادت الضغوط على جنوب السودان بسبب الحرب في السودان، مما أدى إلى نزوح مئات الآلاف. دعا موتيجا إلى تحرك دبلوماسي عاجل من الشركاء الإقليميين والدوليين، مشددًا على ضرورة دعم جهود الوساطة التي يقودها الاتحاد الإفريقي وتجنب إجراء الانتخابات دون توافق سياسي. متحدث باسم منظمة الأمم المتحدة لرعاية الطفولة “يونيسيف”، الثلاثاء، إن ضربات الطائرات المسيّرة تسببت في مقتل وإصابة ثلثي الأطفال ضحايا الحرب في السودان خلال العام الحالي. وبرز استخدام الطائرات المسيّرة كاتجاه تصعيدي في قصف الأسواق والمستشفيات ومحطات الكهرباء ومصادر المياه ومواقع النزوح، وسط تزايد وتيرة استخدامها خلف خطوط النزاع المندلع منذ أبريل 2023. وقال المتحدث باسم يونيسيف جيمس إلدر، في مؤتمر صحفي عُقد في قصر الأمم المتحدة بجنيف بعد زيارته السودان، إن “الطائرات المسيّرة تسببت في ثلثي حالات سقوط الأطفال بين قتيل وجريح خلال هذا العام”. وأوضح أن المسيّرات نقلت الحرب إلى مناطق كانت آمنة في السابق. وأشار إلى أن الشهر السابق شهد تعرض 15 محطة كهرباء للقصف، معتبراً أن هذه الهجمات، التي امتدت جغرافياً ونُفذت بوتيرة متسارعة، تمثل تصعيداً خطيراً في استهداف البنية التحتية المدنية. وأضاف: “دعوني أوضح لماذا يشكل اجتماع الطائرات المسيّرة والجفاف خطراً مميتاً على الأطفال. تعني الكهرباء توفير المياه. فعندما تتعرض محطة للقصف، تتوقف مضخات المياه وتتوقف عمليات معالجة المياه، وتُضطر الأسر إلى اللجوء إلى بدائل مكلفة وغير آمنة. وتنتشر الأمراض”. وبيّن أن استهداف محطات الكهرباء يهدد مرافق التبريد التي تحافظ على صلاحية اللقاحات والأدوية، كما يحرم المزارعين من إمكانية ري محاصيلهم، في ظل النقص الحاد والخانق في الوقود، مما يجعل الغذاء بعيد المنال أمام أعداد متزايدة من الأسر. وفي 24 أكتوبر، قال مفوض الأمم المتحدة السامي لحقوق الإنسان، فولكر تورك، إن 306 سودانيين قُتلوا وأُصيب المئات جراء هجمات الطائرات المسيّرة خلال الأسابيع الثلاثة الأولى من أكتوبر. ورصد مكتب الأمم المتحدة لحقوق الإنسان، بحسب ما أعلنه في 4 سبتمبر الماضي، مقتل 1120 مدنياً نتيجة ضربات بطائرات مسيّرة، بما يمثل أكثر من 80% من إجمالي وفيات المدنيين. وتحدث التصنيف المرحلي المتكامل للأمن الغذائي، في 13 أكتوبر الماضي، عن رصد أكثر من 170 غارة جوية أو حادثة نهب أو اشتباك مسلح في أسواق كردفان خلال العام الحالي، مع تركز النزاع على المجتمعات التي تمتلك الماشية، ومجتمعات الرعاة، والتجمعات الزراعية. وأفاد المتحدث بأن ضربات المسيّرات تحدث رغم التوقعات بأن يعاني نحو 825 ألف طفل دون سن الخامسة من سوء التغذية الحاد الوخيم هذا العام، وهو النوع الذي قد يؤدي إلى الوفاة. وقال جيمس إلدر إن يونيسيف وشركاءها تمكنوا من علاج مئات الآلاف من الأطفال المصابين بأخطر أشكال سوء التغذية فتكاً، إضافة إلى توفير الرعاية الصحية لأكثر من 2. 5 مليون شخص، وتطعيم ملايين الأطفال ضد الأمراض الفتاكة. وأوضح أن يونيسيف أصلحت أنظمة المياه وحولتها إلى العمل بالطاقة الشمسية، ما ساعد على استمرار تدفق المياه الآمنة لنحو 8 ملايين شخص، كما ساعدت ملايين الأطفال على العودة إلى التعلم، فضلاً عن توفير خدمات الحماية والصحة النفسية والدعم النفسي والاجتماعي لنحو 1. 5 مليون طفل وأسرة. ويُقدّر قطاع التغذية التابع للأمم المتحدة أن يحتاج 8.4 مليون من الأطفال دون سن الخامسة والنساء الحوامل والمرضعات في 2026 إلى مساعدات التغذية، منهم نحو 5 ملايين طفل دون سن الخامسة و3.4 ملايين من الحوامل والمرضعات. ويحتاج 4. 19 مليون شخص إلى خدمات علاج سوء التغذية الحاد خلال هذا العام، من بينهم نحو 825 ألف طفل دون سن الخامسة يعانون من سوء التغذية الحاد الوخيم، و2.76 مليون شخص يعانون من سوء التغذية الحاد المتوسط، و599,681 من الحوامل والمرضعات. الكلمات: أطفال السودان الأمم ethiopia.title: Colours, Coffee And Hard Bargaining As Africa Makes Its Mark At COP31
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Colours, Coffee And Hard Bargaining As Africa Makes Its Mark At COP31 - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Colours, Coffee And Hard Bargaining As Africa Makes Its Mark At COP31 Bird Story Agency Ethiopian Coffee 10 November 2026 Bird Story Agency (Africa) By Seth Onyango Africa has brought its colours, coffee and critical minerals to COP31. The last of those could be worth considerably more than all the diplomatic goodwill on offer in Antalya. Africans are hard to miss at COP31. From the colourful prints and flowing robes sweeping through the conference halls to the aroma of freshly brewed Ethiopian coffee, the continent has brought plenty of its character to the Turkish Mediterranean coast. Across the sprawling venue hosting this year's UN climate summit, Africa is making itself seen and heard. There is a dazzling array of fashion, from traditional attire to contemporary designs, and a steady procession of ministers, campaigners, entrepreneurs and negotiators moving between national pavilions and meeting rooms. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Ethiopia has even shipped in traditional stools, utensils and its finest coffee beans, giving visitors a taste of what awaits them when the climate summit moves to Addis Ababa next year. And then there are the minerals. Cobalt from the Democratic Republic of Congo, manganese from South Africa and Gabon, lithium from Zimbabwe and graphite from Mozambique and Tanzania are featuring in conversations about Africa's place in the global energy transition. Several African delegates and experts speaking to bird story agency in Antalya see these resources as a source of leverage in discussions over investment, technology and the industries that will supply the world's growing demand for clean energy. The Democratic Republic of Congo supplies much of the world's cobalt, a mineral used in rechargeable batteries, while African producers also hold substantial deposits of lithium, graphite and manganese. These resources are important to manufacturers of electric vehicles, batteries and electricity storage systems. African governments are seeking investment in processing facilities, factories and electricity infrastructure that would allow producing countries to retain more of the value generated by these resources. The Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia have pursued cooperation on battery materials and electric vehicle supply chains, while Zimbabwe has introduced measures intended to encourage more domestic processing of lithium. Such plans depend on reliable electricity, transport infrastructure, technical expertise and access to finance. They are also bringing trade and industrial development into discussions that have traditionally focused heavily on emissions reductions and climate finance. Those financing demands were among the first issues to cause disagreement when negotiations opened in Antalya. African countries sought dedicated discussions on tripling adaptation finance, the future financing needs of the Green Climate Fund and the effects of climate-related trade measures on developing economies. A proposal for a separate agenda item on adaptation finance failed to secure consensus on Monday, leaving negotiators to pursue the issue through other parts of the conference. Ethiopia brings Addis Ababa to Antalya At Ethiopia's pavilion, preparations for next year's summit are already under way. Traditional stools, decorative pieces and jebena coffee pots have been brought from home, creating a space where visitors can experience the country's coffee ceremony while learning about its climate and development programmes. Ethiopia is preparing to host COP32 in Addis Ababa in 2027, returning the annual negotiations to Africa for the first time since COP27 in Egypt. The pavilion opened on Monday with Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos, the incoming COP32 president, and Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa, who will serve as chief negotiator for next year's conference. Timothewos has already begun setting out Ethiopia's approach to the presidency. Addressing the COP31 plenary, he called for stronger international climate cooperation, faster implementation of existing commitments and action to address financing gaps. Ethiopia has pledged to oversee a fair, transparent and inclusive process when it assumes the presidency. The country is also using its presence in Antalya to promote renewable energy, climate-resilient agriculture and its Green Legacy tree-planting programme. Its substantial hydropower resources form part of plans to expand electricity generation and attract investment into manufacturing and other industries. The coffee ceremony has become a distinctive feature of the pavilion, offering visitors a chance to experience one of the country's best-known traditions. For Ethiopia, preparations for COP32 are taking place alongside discussions about the investment and international partnerships it hopes to attract. Investment moves up the African agenda The wider African presence at COP31 includes development banks, trade institutions and businesses seeking investment in energy, infrastructure and manufacturing. At the Africa Pavilion, the African Development Bank, African Union Commission, United Nations Economic Commission for Africa, African Union Development Agency (AUDA-NEPAD) and African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) have gathered under the theme Turning Climate Commitments into Investments . Their programme covers renewable energy, critical minerals, carbon markets, climate finance and industrial development. Afreximbank's participation brings trade finance and regional supply chains into the discussions, particularly as African countries seek to expand manufacturing under the African Continental Free Trade Area. Mineral processing, battery manufacturing and other energy-intensive industries require large, reliable electricity supplies. The COP31 presidency has placed electrification among its major initiatives, proposing to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption from about 23 per cent to 35 per cent by 2035. The proposal comes as African governments seek to expand electricity access for roughly 600 million people in sub-Saharan Africa who remain without power. The World Bank and African Development Bank are already working through Mission 300, which aims to connect 300 million Africans to electricity by 2030. On Tuesday, the COP31 presidency announced a new international electrification finance coalition, with the two banks set to serve as its inaugural co-chairs in 2027. The initiative is intended to bring together governments, development banks and private financial institutions to mobilise investment in electricity infrastructure across emerging and developing economies. COP31 President of Negotiations Chris Bowen has acknowledged the importance of investment in delivering the proposed electrification target. "Ambition matters, but it must be backed by investment, infrastructure and implementation," Bowen said. For African countries, borrowing costs, currency risks and the financial condition of national utilities remain major obstacles to expanding electricity generation and transmission networks. These constraints also affect the industrial projects that governments hope will attract investment around the continent's mineral resources. The first dispute is over finance Inside the negotiating rooms, the African Group of Negotiators has been pressing for progress on adaptation finance, the just transition and the resources needed to implement national climate commitments. The group's chair, Nana Dr Antwi-Boasiako Amoah of Ghana, has identified finance as one of Africa's principal priorities at COP31. At COP30 in Belém, countries agreed to at least triple adaptation finance for developing economies by 2035. African governments want clarity on how that commitment will be implemented, including the amount of finance to be provided, the sources of funding and the arrangements for monitoring delivery. Their request for a dedicated adaptation finance agenda item failed to gain consensus during the opening discussions in Antalya. Amoah expressed dissatisfaction with the outcome and indicated that African negotiators would continue pursuing the issue through other negotiating channels. The Green Climate Fund is another area of concern, with African countries seeking greater certainty over the resources available to support adaptation and the implementation of national climate plans. Many African governments are already dealing with high debt repayments while trying to finance infrastructure, agriculture, electricity and public services. The terms on which international climate finance is provided can therefore affect how much governments can invest in protecting communities from floods, droughts and other climate impacts. African negotiators are also seeking discussions on climate-related trade measures. As major economies introduce rules linked to the carbon emissions associated with imported products, African manufacturers face new requirements that could affect their access to international markets. These developments are particularly relevant to countries seeking to expand mineral processing and other industrial activities that depend on affordable electricity. Heat puts health products to the test Elsewhere at the summit, South African medical doctor and climate-health advocate Dr Nompumelelo Nkosi-Ntombela was following discussions about the effects of rising temperatures on essential medicines. Nkosi-Ntombela, who serves on the KwaZulu-Natal Climate Change and Sustainable Development Council, attended a high-level panel on climate-sensitive health technologies during the summit's opening Health Day. The discussions included a project examining how extreme heat and humidity affect medicines and diagnostic products used in countries already experiencing high temperatures. Unitaid has announced a US$10.9 million programme, known as SHIELD, to investigate the heat stability of essential health products, including medicines used to treat HIV, tuberculosis and malaria. The project will study storage and transport conditions in Kenya, Nigeria, Senegal and India, with findings validated in South Africa and Brazil. The research is scheduled to run from 2027 to 2030. For Nkosi-Ntombela, the initiative addresses a concern for health systems where high temperatures, unreliable electricity and long transport routes can complicate the safe storage and distribution of medicines. "Climate change is a health conversation too," she said, reflecting on her first day at COP31. She also called for greater involvement of women and young people in climate and health programmes, particularly in communities where access to essential services is limited. The SHIELD project will examine how heat and humidity affect the quality of health products and identify ways to protect them during storage and transport. Its findings could inform improvements in packaging, temperature monitoring and medical supply chains. Campaigners press for grants Financing has also been a central concern for African civil society organisations attending the summit. Greenpeace Africa is among the groups calling for more grant-based climate finance, greater investment in renewable energy and stronger accountability for major polluters. Ferdinand Omondi, a strategic communications and policy specialist associated with Greenpeace Africa, has raised concerns about the technical language surrounding international climate finance and the difficulty communities face in understanding what the agreements mean for them. He has pointed to the difference between a Kenyan farmer receiving a commercial loan to recover from drought and receiving public grant financing as an example of how international decisions can affect people already experiencing climate impacts. Greenpeace Africa is advocating grants rather than additional debt, alongside faster renewable energy deployment and measures to hold major polluters financially accountable. Similar demands have been made by a coalition of civil society organisations pressing the COP31 presidency to strengthen its proposed electrification framework. In an open letter updated ahead of the summit, more than 120 organisations called for significantly increased public climate finance, with grants and concessional funding directed towards developing economies. The signatories also want financing to reach smaller enterprises, community energy providers and local organisations, alongside measures to improve affordability and electricity access. Their proposals include stronger protections for communities affected by mineral extraction and greater investment in local manufacturing and technology transfer. The demands intersect with several issues being discussed by African governments, from electricity access and industrial development to climate adaptation and the management of natural resources. From Antalya to Addis Ababa COP31 continues until November 20, with African negotiators seeking progress on adaptation finance, the just transition and the financing arrangements needed to implement national climate commitments. The opening dispute over adaptation finance has left one of the continent's priorities to be addressed through other parts of the negotiations. Meanwhile, African governments and development institutions are pursuing investment in renewable electricity, manufacturing, mineral processing and regional trade. The continent's mineral resources have become an important part of discussions about the industries that will supply the global energy transition. Developing those industries will require electricity, infrastructure, financing and commercial partnerships, with African governments seeking arrangements that allow more processing and manufacturing to take place locally. Ethiopia will host the next round of negotiations in Addis Ababa, where many of these issues are likely to remain on the agenda. Its officials have already begun preparations in Antalya, meeting international partners and promoting the country's climate and development programmes. For now, African delegates face days of meetings, investment discussions and negotiations. At the Ethiopian pavilion, visitors are still being welcomed with freshly prepared coffee. Speaking at the International Partners Day marked at the Defense Peacekeeping Center in Addis Ababa today, the head noted that Ethiopia's contributions to global peace span decades beginning with the Korean War in 1951 and extending through missions in the Congo, Rwanda, Liberia, Burundi, Darfur, Abyei, South Sudan, and Somalia. The nation's long history of peacekeeping is rooted in professionalism, discipline, and profound sacrifice, Major General Adamneh stated, reaffirming Ethiopia's continued commitment to foster global peace and security. Underscoring the nation's deep-rooted role in collective security as a founding member of the United Nations and the African Union, the Center Head paid tribute to the peacekeepers that lost their lives in the line of duty. "Their ultimate sacrifice will forever be etched in the history of our shared journey," Major General Adamneh stated. Commandant of the International Peace Support Training Institute (IPSTI), Brigadier General Gezahegn Fikadu noted the institute's expanding role as an African center of excellence. The institute equips military, police, and civilian personnel for complex UN, EU, and regional operations through generic, specialized, and mission-specific training, he said. "IPSTI aspires to serve as an important platform for translating Ethiopia's wealth of practical experience into professional knowledge, skills, research, and training opportunities for the wider African and international peace support community." Noting that modern peace support operations demand deepened collaboration, shared technology, and sustainable institutional backing, Brigadier General Gezahegn emphasized the need for strengthening local and international partners to collaborate on joint training, research, logistical support, and regional standby force development. Major General Teshome Gemechu, Main Directorate Director of Defense International Relations and Military Cooperation at the Ministry of Defense, for his part emphasized the need to renew spirit of partnership to secure a more peaceful and stable future for Africa and the world. Enhanced partnership provides a strong foundation for continued operations, he stated, calling on partners to maintain the spirit of cooperation by working together, sharing new knowledge, and helping each other in different modalities. ethiopia.title: The World I Taught, the War I Witnessed - a Personal Reckoning With the Erosion of International Law in Tigray
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: The World I Taught, the War I Witnessed - a Personal Reckoning With the Erosion of International Law in Tigray - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: The World I Taught, the War I Witnessed - a Personal Reckoning With the Erosion of International Law in Tigray 10 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) opinion Addis Abeba — For more than two decades as an academic staff member at Mekelle University, I stood before lecture halls filled with young, eager minds teaching political science and thought of the promises of a better future. In those classrooms, I taught my students about the post-Cold War new world order, the sacred duty of international law, and the indispensability of international organizations in preserving human dignity. Beyond academia, as the former board chair and member of the Ethiopian Red Cross Society Tigray Region branch, the principles of humanitarian assistance were not merely textbook concepts to me--they were a lived, solemn vow. International Humanitarian Law (IHL), the legal framework governing human behavior in its most destructive state, was born not out of abstract philosophy but from raw, unvarnished horror. In 1859, Swiss businessman Henry Dunant witnessed the devastating aftermath of the Battle of Solferino , where over 40,000 dead and wounded soldiers lay abandoned without basic medical care. Horrified, Dunant organized local villagers under the simple banner Tutti fratelli ("All are brothers") to treat the suffering regardless of their uniform. His memoir, A Memory of Solferino , catalyzed two historic milestones: the founding of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) in 1863 and the adoption of the First Geneva Convention in 1864. For the first time, sovereign states established written rules governing conduct during wartime, recognizing medical personnel as neutral and guaranteeing humane treatment for wounded combatants. As weapons became increasingly lethal, international humanitarian law evolved to address emerging threats and establish clearer limits on the conduct of war. The Hague Conventions (1899 and 1907) restricted the use of certain weapons and military tactics, prohibiting chemical agents, poison, and weapons designed to cause unnecessary suffering. The Four Geneva Conventions (1949) expanded protections in the aftermath of World War II to cover naval combatants, prisoners of war, and civilian populations. The UN Charter (1945) and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) established the prohibition of aggressive war ( jus ad bellum ) while affirming the inherent dignity of every human being and laying the foundation for its protection under international law. The Rome Statute (1998) established the International Criminal Court (ICC) , codifying war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide while reinforcing individual accountability for commanders and heads of state. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Together, these instruments established an unequivocal legal benchmark: Even war has limits. I brought these principles into my classroom daily, persuading my students that humanity had made a permanent shift. However, recent conflicts spanning Palestine, Tigray, Sudan, Rwanda, Iraq, Yemen, and Ukraine reveal a glaring discrepancy between the solemn oaths of IHL and the plight of unarmed civilians. This reality compels me to question the genuine commitment of the international community to human dignity. Are wars truly governed by international law? If so, why do these laws remain ineffective in practice? Even war has limits." Theoretically, conflict does not suspend humanity or abolish the treaties that states agreed must govern the ethics of warfare. Yet unarmed civilians continue to be killed, displaced, denied medical supplies, and uprooted from their homelands. Millions of children are left without caretakers, and countless women are systematically targeted with sexual violence. According to official UNHCR global figures , over 117.8 million people remain forcibly displaced worldwide--including 68.7 million internally displaced persons and 35.5 million refugees. These figures expose the severe enforcement crisis facing IHL today. It is true that war has laws, but having these laws means little if signatory states fail to implement and enforce them. In recent conflicts, IHL bodies have often been reduced to issuing press releases that cannot save lives, prevent displacement, or stop mass atrocities, ethnic cleansing, and genocide. The Global Breakdown: Half-decade of unchecked atrocity The past half-decade has delivered an agonizing reckoning for those of us who believed in the post-Cold War promise. Across multiple battlefields, armed actors have turned civilian populations from incidental victims into intentional targets, deploying starvation, total siege, and indiscriminate bombardment as standard doctrines. In Ukraine, the re-emergence of large-scale interstate war brought systematic strikes on power grids and residential blocks , displacing millions. In Gaza, urban warfare reached an unprecedented density of destruction, leveling residential quarters and dismantling critical medical safeguards under sustained bombardment. In Sudan, rival military factions turned major metropolitan areas into free-fire zones, triggering widespread ethnic killings in Darfur and uprooting millions. As a father who wishes above all else for a bright, peaceful, and secure future for my daughters, watching this global unraveling breaks my heart. I used to tell my young students that international law existed to protect their future; today, fathers across the globe are forced to watch their children suffer under the weight of unpunished war crimes. Among these defining crises of our era, the conflict in Tigray serves as a stark, deeply personal testament to how total siege, high-tech remote violence, and geopolitical neglect converge to break the international rule of law. While the UN Security Council has convened several times and issued numerous statements, declarations alone have proven powerless to ensure safety, deliver humanitarian assistance, or avert tragedy. The Tigray Crucible: Siege, weaponized starvation, and broken peace During the 2020-2022 war, I was in Tigray. I personally witnessed gross violations of human rights, people dying from starvation and lack of medicine, families torn apart, and Tigray disconnected from the outside world under a complete 360-degree blockade imposed by the federal government and allied forces. Hundreds of thousands of civilians lost their lives, over a million were displaced, thousands of women suffered sexual violence, and essential social infrastructure was methodically dismantled. This devastating campaign did not materialize out of thin air in November 2020. It was preceded by state-led rhetoric that systematically dehumanized Tigrayans. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed publicly characterized Tigrayan leaders as "day-hyenas," while his advisor Daniel Kibret called for the eradication of Tigrayans, describing them as "cancers" and "weeds" in need of removal . Despite these unmistakable warning signs of impending genocide, the international community was celebrating its diplomatic honeymoon with the prime minister, having awarded him the 2019 Nobel Peace Prize . When conflict erupted, international actors issued mild statements while watching the horror unfold like scenes in a movie. The war brought together the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF), Eritrean forces, regional state troops, and Amhara militias in a brutal military campaign. Rather than adhering to international humanitarian law (IHL), the combatants employed tactics that directly threatened the population's biological and social survival through a systematic blockade. Banking services were frozen by the central authorities, cutting people off from their savings, trade, and diaspora remittances, resulting in severe cash shortages and the breakdown of markets. Telecommunications, internet services, and news media were also shut down, isolating millions of people and obstructing efforts to document human rights abuses. Meanwhile, access to fuel, medicine, and food aid was severely restricted, contributing to widespread famine and the near-total collapse of the healthcare system. Such measures directly violate core tenets of international law, notably Article 54 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions , which strictly prohibits starving civilians and destroying objects indispensable to their survival. Personal grief, atrocity documentation, and renewed crisis This tragedy was not an abstract academic case study for me--it shattered my life completely. Because of the war and the collapse of healthcare, I lost my beloved wife, along with many dear relatives and colleagues. Amid this profound grief, I was called to lead the Commission of Inquiry on Tigray Genocide (CITG), tasked with documenting the raw human atrocities, civilian suffering, and physical destruction inflicted upon our region. Every testimony of agony I recorded solidified my conviction: such horrors must never be repeated--not in Tigray, not anywhere in Ethiopia, and not anywhere in the world. As a member of the Tigray Public Diplomacy Council--a civic initiative composed of academics, civic leaders, and diaspora representatives dedicated to regional stability--I worked relentlessly to foster dialogue and build a path toward peace. Lasting stability requires putting human rights and international humanitarian law above political, military, and economic ambitions" When the November 2022 Pretoria Cessation of Hostilities Agreement (CoHA) was signed between the Ethiopian federal government and the TPLF, it brought a brief glimmer of hope. However, key provisions--including full disarmament, the complete withdrawal of non-federal forces, the return of displaced persons, and genuine accountability--stalled. Internal political fragmentation within Tigray, combined with a lack of federal commitment to fully implement the Pretoria accord, steadily escalated tensions. Recently, renewed military hostilities and security escalations have once again erupted across parts of Tigray. Heavy artillery and ground clashes have displaced thousands, while organizations such as Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) report treating hundreds of wounded civilians in regional facilities. With communications and services disrupted once more, the trauma returned instantly. When lines went dark, I found myself unable to reach relatives and colleagues in Mekelle, paralyzed by anxiety for their safety. Subduing geopolitics for global peace, reclaiming the rule of law The systemic failure to enforce compliance in Tigray, Sudan, Ukraine, and Gaza is fundamentally a crisis of political will. Power rivalries, strategic alliances, and economic interests too often lead international bodies and influential states to apply International Humanitarian Law (IHL) selectively. As I recently argued in Addis Standard regarding the U.S. decision to lift sanctions on Ethiopia and Eritrea , prioritizing strategic partnerships over principled accountability sets a dangerous precedent. When global powers prematurely replace accountability with impunity, it signals to warring factions worldwide that severe violations of international law carry no lasting consequences. Violations of international norms in one conflict can become precedents for combatants elsewhere, gradually eroding established standards of conduct. Accountability also weakens when the UN Security Council and regional bodies are paralyzed by political deadlock, vetoes, or strategic alliances, allowing impunity to flourish. Moreover, human lives risk being valued according to political or geopolitical considerations, creating a hierarchy of victims. Yet a victim in Mekelle, Khartoum, or Gaza deserves the same legal protection as a victim in Kyiv. Humanitarian law was constructed to function universally, independent of political alliances or strategic convenience. Allowing political interests to dictate when the Geneva Conventions apply undermines the credibility of the entire international order. The founding of the Red Cross in 1863 and the first Geneva treaty in 1864 proved that humanity could establish shared rules even amid intense conflict. Rebuilding that consensus today is an urgent necessity for global security. For Tigray and active conflicts worldwide, lasting stability requires putting human rights and international humanitarian law above political, military, and economic ambitions. Ending blockades, enforcing strict target verification in drone warfare, providing unhindered humanitarian access, and holding perpetrators accountable across all sides are not optional gestures; they are binding obligations under international law. Having taught these principles in the classroom, organized relief on the ground, documented devastating losses as a commission lead, and personally borne the unbearable loss of my wife and relatives, I know the real human cost when these laws are ignored. If we allow power and political expediency to dictate survival, we discard the hard-won lessons of history and condemn our children, including my own daughters, to a world without mercy. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Allied Gold Pours First Gold At Ethiopia's Kurmuk Mine, Targets Commercial Production By Year-End - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Allied Gold Pours First Gold At Ethiopia's Kurmuk Mine, Targets Commercial Production By Year-End 10 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Canadian mining company Allied Gold has poured its first gold at the Kurmuk mine in Ethiopia's Benishangul-Gumuz Regional State, marking a major milestone for the project as the company targets commercial production by the end of 2026. The first gold pour transitions Kurmuk into production, making it Allied Gold's newest and lowest-cost operation, according to Mining Technology , which reported the development on 10 November. The company said installation of the remaining power infrastructure and mobilisation of its full haulage fleet were still underway, with both expected to be completed this month. Allied Gold aims to bring the mine to its full designed capacity in early 2027, with gold recovery rates expected to increase progressively through 2026. The company projects production of between 25,000 and 35,000 ounces this year, rising to between 240,000 and 270,000 ounces in 2027 and approximately 300,000 ounces in 2028. The company expects average annual production of around 300,000 ounces during the mine's first four years, before stabilising at approximately 240,000 ounces annually over the remainder of its operating life. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Allied Gold's management and board of directors credited the project's Ethiopian and international teams, as well as the Ethiopian government, for supporting its development. The company described Kurmuk as one of the country's first large-scale mechanised mining operations. The milestone follows growing international investment interest in the project. On 20 August, Addis Standard reported that China's Zijin Gold International had acquired a 9.2% stake in Allied Gold for nearly $300 million, giving it partial ownership of the company's mining portfolio, including Kurmuk. The investment followed the collapse of an earlier proposed $4 billion acquisition of Allied Gold by Zijin after the companies failed to secure Chinese regulatory approval. The two companies subsequently proceeded with the minority shareholding agreement. Allied Gold, which also operates mines in Mali and Côte d'Ivoire, projects consolidated production of between 400,000 and 435,000 ounces in 2026, increasing to between 615,000 and 670,000 ounces in 2027. It aims to raise annual output to approximately 800,000 ounces by 2029, supported partly by expansion at its Sadiola mine. Allied Gold had been advancing exploration at Kurmuk ahead of the latest production milestone. In December 2025, the company announced five new exploration targets at the project, saying drilling results had strengthened its prospects for developing a high-volume, long-life gold operation. ethiopia.title: Food Shortages Hit 71 Percent of Ethiopian Families Displaced Into Kenya's Moyale
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Food Shortages Hit 71 Percent of Ethiopian Families Displaced Into Kenya's Moyale - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Food Shortages Hit 71 Percent of Ethiopian Families Displaced Into Kenya's Moyale 10 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Tens of thousands of people who fled escalating conflict in Moyale along Ethiopia's border between Oromia and Somali regional states and crossed into northern Kenya are facing acute food shortages, inadequate shelter and limited access to clean water and healthcare, according to a new assessment by the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and humanitarian partners. An estimated 50,000 people had arrived in Kenya's Moyale area as of 29 October following weeks of fighting in Ethiopia's Borana and surrounding areas, many arriving with few belongings and relying on already resource-constrained host communities for basic necessities. The conflict erupted in Ethiopia's Moyale town on 18 October following a dispute over the opening of a Somali Regional State administration office and the raising of its flag. The dispute triggered an exchange of gunfire between Somali regional forces and Oromia local militias, leaving 13-year-old Diqqoo Jaataan Aagaa dead. Residents gave conflicting accounts of the circumstances surrounding the girl's death, with some accusing Somali regional police of shooting her, while others said she was caught in crossfire. However, the incident triggered protests, transport disruptions and the closure of businesses before escalating into wider armed confrontations. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Fighting intensified on 22 October, with heavy exchanges of gunfire reported in several parts of Moyale, including Malab, Chamuk, Bole, Kebele 01 and Waqo Dogo. The clashes subsequently spread to Gumi Eldallo, Wachile and Arero districts in the East Borana Zone, with reports of burned homes, civilian casualties and mass displacement, Addis Standard reported. In its latest reporting on 4 November, A ddis Standard said fighting had continued in seven districts, with particularly intense clashes around the Dawa River basin. Attempts at mediation between the two sides had failed to produce a lasting agreement, while residents expressed fears of further displacement and casualties. The IOM assessment, conducted between 29 and 30 October by the Kenyan government and Marsabit County administration, with support from UN agencies and humanitarian organizations, found that 71% of surveyed households did not have enough food, while 80% identified food as their most urgent need. "Families who fled are facing serious shortages of food, water and adequate shelter, while communities hosting them are already facing limited resources," said Nomagugu Ncube, IOM Kenya Chief of Mission, calling for assistance to reach both displaced families and their host communities. Nearly all households surveyed (96%) had fled Ethiopia, mainly from the Oromia and Somali regions. Nine in 10 respondents said their entire village had fled, indicating the extensive scale of displacement. Children account for more than half of the displaced population, including a significant number under the age of five, raising concerns over their health and well-being amid worsening living conditions. Access to safe drinking water and sanitation also remains severely constrained. Some 44% of surveyed households reported insufficient access to drinking water, while more than three-quarters said they had no handwashing facilities. Conditions were particularly difficult at temporary displacement sites in Somare, Taqwa Mosque and St. Mary's Catholic, where access to water and sanitation was severely limited. Healthcare access is another major concern, with more than half of surveyed households reporting difficulties reaching nearby health facilities, mainly due to high costs and shortages of medicines. Most displaced families are staying with relatives or other members of host communities, placing additional pressure on already limited household resources. Others have sought refuge in schools and temporary sites, while some are sleeping in the open. OM and humanitarian partners are calling for urgent funding to scale up food assistance, emergency shelter, clean water, sanitation and healthcare for displaced families and the communities hosting them. The partnership marks a significant step towards strengthening air transport connectivity across Africa and expanding travel opportunities for passengers. Accordingly, Ethiopian Airlines and Air Peace will collaborate through a bilateral interline arrangement covering both passenger travel and checked baggage services. The partnership enables each airline to issue tickets for eligible itineraries that include flights operated by both carriers, providing customers with a more convenient and integrated travel experience. Through this collaboration, passengers will be able to book qualifying journeys on a single ticket and enjoy through-checked baggage to their destination, where applicable. The streamlined process eliminates the need for separate bookings and baggage re-checks, creating a smoother and more efficient travel experience. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The agreement links Air Peace's domestic and regional network with Ethiopian Airlines' vast international network spanning Africa, Europe, Asia, the Middle East, and the Americas. As a result, travelers departing from major Nigerian and west African cities will gain seamless access to Ethiopian Airlines' global destinations through Addis Ababa, while international passengers arriving on Ethiopian Airlines flights will benefit from expanded onward travel options across Nigeria and west Africa through Air Peace's domestic network. Commenting on the partnership, Ethiopian Airlines Group CEO, Mesfin Tasew said, "We are delighted to partner with Air Peace, a leading carrier in Nigeria, through this strategic interline agreement. This collaboration reflects our shared commitment to enhancing connectivity, improving customer convenience, and supporting the growth of air travel across the African continent. By combining our strengths, we are creating more travel opportunities and bringing Africa closer to the world." Dr. Allen Onyema, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Air Peace said, "This partnership with Ethiopian Airlines represents another significant milestone in our commitment to strengthening Africa's aviation connectivity and bringing the continent closer together. By combining Air Peace's extensive domestic, regional network, and our growing international network with Ethiopian Airlines' global reach, we are creating greater opportunities for seamless travel in and out of the African continent. Beyond expanding travel options, this collaboration reflects our shared vision of fostering stronger economic, commercial and cultural ties across Africa and beyond. At Air Peace, we remain committed to building strategic partnerships that enhance passenger convenience, broaden connectivity and position African aviation as a formidable force in global air transport." Speaking at the International Partners Day marked at the Defense Peacekeeping Center in Addis Ababa today, the head noted that Ethiopia’s contributions to global peace span decades beginning with the Korean War in 1951 and extending through missions in the Congo, Rwanda, Liberia, Burundi, Darfur, Abyei, South Sudan, and Somalia. The nation’s long history of peacekeeping is rooted in professionalism, discipline, and profound sacrifice, Major General Adamneh stated, reaffirming Ethiopia’s continued commitment to foster global peace and security. Underscoring the nation's deep-rooted role in collective security as a founding member of the United Nations and the African Union, the Center Head paid tribute to the peacekeepers that lost their lives in the line of duty. He recalled that 4 personnel tragically lost their lives in South Sudan in 2026 alone. "Their ultimate sacrifice will forever be etched in the history of our shared journey," Major General Adamneh stated. Commandant of the International Peace Support Training Institute (IPSTI), Brigadier General Gezahegn Fikadu noted the institute’s expanding role as an African center of excellence. The institute equips military, police, and civilian personnel for complex UN, EU, and regional operations through generic, specialized, and mission-specific training, he said. "IPSTI aspires to serve as an important platform for translating Ethiopia's wealth of practical experience into professional knowledge, skills, research, and training opportunities for the wider African and international peace support community." Noting that modern peace support operations demand deepened collaboration, shared technology, and sustainable institutional backing, Brigadier General Gezahegn emphasized the need for strengthening local and international partners to collaborate on joint training, research, logistical support, and regional standby force development. Major General Teshome Gemechu, Main Directorate Director of Defense International Relations and Military Cooperation at the Ministry of Defense, for his part emphasized the need to renew spirit of partnership to secure a more peaceful and stable future for Africa and the world. Enhanced partnership provides a strong foundation for continued operations, he stated, calling on partners to maintain the spirit of cooperation by working together, sharing new knowledge, and helping each other in different modalities. The International Partners Day was marked along with partners, including military attaches of various countries and representatives of international organizations under the theme “Invest in Peace: Building Resilient Partnerships for Global Security”. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden

PHOTO | COURTESY Audio By Vocalize Principal Secretary for the State Department for Internal Security and National Administration Raymond Omollo has said Kenya is monitoring increased security risks as Ethiopian refugees flock Moyale. Omollo said on Tuesday that refugees coming to the country had put the security sector under pressure. “This security situation, where different groups are fighting, we've had cases of stray bullets coming into the Kenyan side,” Omollo told NTV. “The Inspector General of police was there at the end of last week together with a team from the national government administration just to calm the situation and manage it." The PS argued that an increase in population of refugees can lead to disease outbreak thus working towards having enough medical supplies. “We are looking at medical supplies, particularly to address the issues around disease outbreak if it gets to that point,” he added. He also confirmed the continued security monitoring by having active conversations between Kenyan and Ethiopian officials. “Most importantly is community engagement and sensitization so that then even as there is escalation or movement, then we don't have the locals feeling like they are being pushed to act so that then we have retaliation or something like that,” he insisted. Omollo added that Moyale leaders had also been engaged in these conversations. somalia.title: Unlocking Somalia's Investment Potential- Opportunities in the Blue Economy, Fisheries, Energy and Agriculture - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Unlocking Somalia's Investment Potential- Opportunities in the Blue Economy, Fisheries, Energy and Agriculture - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME OPINION Unlocking Somalia's Investment Potential- Opportunities in the Blue Economy, Fisheries, Energy and Agriculture Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Guleid Osman Tuesday November 10, 2026 Debt relief, regional integration and a new investment law have repositioned Somalia as an early-mover market. This article examines the domestic and foreign investment opportunities across four connected sectors the blue economy, fisheries, energy, and agriculture and the conditions under which they can be realized. Introduction For much of the past three decades, Somalia has been discussed in terms of fragility rather than opportunity. That framing is becoming outdated. Since reaching the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) Completion Point in December 2023, the country has eliminated almost all of its legacy external debt, joined the East African Community, and enacted the Somalia Investment Law 2025. Foreign direct investment has risen steadily, reaching US$834 million in 2025, while the Somali diaspora transfers more than US$3 billion a year in personal remittances alone. The opportunities are substantial and interlinked. Somalia possesses the longest coastline on mainland Africa, fish stocks that are harvested at a fraction of their sustainable yield, some of the continent's strongest solar and wind resources, and a livestock export trade that crossed the billion-dollar mark in 2025. At the same time, electricity remains among the most expensive in the world, cold-chain infrastructure is almost absent, and only a small share of irrigable land is cultivated. This article argues that the greatest value lies at the intersection of these sectors. Affordable renewable power makes cold storage viable; cold storage makes fish and meat exportable; and modernized ports convert exportable products into foreign-exchange earnings. Investors—domestic, diaspora and foreign—who approach Somalia's economy as a connected system rather than as isolated sectors are best placed to capture that value. The Investment Climate Somalia's macroeconomic position has changed fundamentally in the past three years. In December 2023 the Executive Boards of the IMF and the World Bank's International Development Association approved the country's HIPC Completion Point, reducing external public debt from US$5.3 billion at end-2018 to approximately US$0.6 billion and unlocking about US$4.5 billion in debt service relief (IMF). Weeks earlier, Somalia had been admitted to the East African Community, giving Somali producers preferential access to a regional market of roughly 300 million people (The EastAfrican). The economy is growing, though more slowly than before. Real GDP expanded by 4.1 percent in 2024; the IMF projects 3.0 percent for 2025 and 3.3 percent for 2026, citing reduced foreign aid and adverse weather as the principal constraints (Ecofin Agency). Nominal GDP is estimated at about US$14.2 billion in 2026 (IMF World Economic Outlook, via Fermor). Fiscal policy remains anchored by an IMF Extended Credit Facility, under which disbursements have reached US$100 million, and the Fund has noted progress in Central Bank supervision and preparations to reintroduce the Somali shilling (Channel Africa). Investor interest has followed. According to UNCTAD's World Investment Report 2026, FDI inflows rose from US$601 million in 2021 to US$834 million in 2025, while the stock of foreign investment grew from US$4.3 billion to US$7.2 billion over the same period (Dawan Africa). Relative to the size of the economy, these inflows are significant: World Bank data put FDI at 6.4 percent of GDP in 2024 (World Bank WDI). The legal framework has matured in parallel. The Somalia Investment Law 2025 provides a clearer and more predictable basis for foreign participation, and the Somalia Investment Promotion Agency (SOMINVEST) serves as the principal point of entry. Somalia has been a member of the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency since March 2020, making political-risk insurance available to foreign investors (World Bank), and a public–private partnership law has been in preparation since debt relief was secured. The Blue Economy: Ports, Logistics and Offshore Resources Somalia's 3,333-kilometre coastline and approximately one million square kilometers of maritime territory lie alongside the shipping lanes linking the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean (US Commercial Service). Geography alone makes the country a natural candidate for maritime trade, transshipment and logistics. The investable opportunities fall broadly into three categories: port infrastructure and associated free zones, services linked to offshore energy exploration, and a range of smaller coastal enterprises. Ports and Free Zones Port development has already attracted the largest single foreign investments in the country. At Berbera, DP World operates a 30-year concession that began in 2017 and carries a planned investment of up to US$442 million across two phases, including a new quay, an expanded container yard and the Berbera Economic Zone (Gulf News). At Bosaso, a 30-year concession agreed with Puntland envisages a US$336 million multipurpose upgrade, also in two phases (Trade Arabia). The Port of Mogadishu, managed by Turkey's Albayrak Group, is one of the Federal Government's largest sources of domestic revenue, and in July 2026 the President discussed plans for an entirely new port to meet the capital's growing needs (Dawan Africa). Smaller ports, including Kismayo, Hobyo and Garacad which received its first vessel in 2022—have also attracted interest from public and private investors (Maritime Executive). Across all these facilities the constraints are similar: insufficient berths, warehousing, cold storage, cargo-handling equipment and professional management. Each of these gaps represents a contract-sized opportunity accessible to domestic logistics firms that need not finance an entire concession. Offshore Oil and Gas Somalia's offshore hydrocarbon potential has long attracted speculation; it is now being tested. Under a 2024 intergovernmental framework, the Turkish Petroleum Corporation (TPAO) acquired 3D seismic data across Blocks 142, 152 and 153 and began drilling the Curad-1 exploration well in Block 153 in April 2026 (Oil Price). The reported fiscal terms are favorable to the operator, with royalties capped at 5 percent and cost recovery of up to 90 percent of production—an explicit trade-off of early revenue for reduced exploration risk. Resource estimates of 30 billion barrels or more remain un-risked and unproven (bne Intelli News). For most investors, the realistic near-term opportunity lies not in upstream equity but in supporting services: supply bases, logistics, fuel storage and local-content provision. Coastal Enterprise Beyond ports and hydrocarbons, the blue economy offers a range of smaller opportunities well suited to domestic and diaspora capital. These include ship chandlery, bunkering and repair services, particularly at Bosaso and Berbera; coastal tourism and hospitality, which the Ministry of Foreign Affairs identifies as a largely overlooked sector (Ministry of Foreign Affairs); and salt production, seaweed cultivation and desalination. Fisheries: Closing the Gap Between Catch and Potential Few sectors illustrate the distance between Somalia's resources and its realized output as clearly as fisheries. According to data submitted to the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission, the national catch reached 76,026 tons in 2024, a 30 percent increase on the previous year, of which yellowfin tuna accounted for 18,635 tons (Dawan Africa). Estimates of sustainable yield vary considerably but are uniformly higher: the US Commercial Service cites a potential well above 200,000 tons a year (US Commercial Service), the Ministry of Foreign Affairs refers to some 300,000 tons of fish and 10,000 tons of crustaceans (Ministry of Foreign Affairs), and a 2025 analysis by the Somali Development and Reconstruction Bank places the figure between 380,000 and 500,000 tons. Meanwhile, illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing is estimated to cost the country around US$300 million annually (Daily Maverick). The constraint, in short, is not the resource but the vessels, ice, storage, processing capacity and market access needed to capture it onshore. An Improving Policy Environment Several recent policy developments have strengthened the case for investment. In March 2026 the Ministry of Fisheries and Blue Economy published revised exclusive economic zone license fees for foreign-flagged vessels and for Somali-flagged vessels not wholly owned by Somali citizens; crucially, companies that invest in onshore economic activity within the same fishing year may qualify for discounted fees (Ministry of Fisheries and Blue Economy). This rewards landing and processing in Somalia rather than at sea. Foreign vessels remain excluded from the first 24 nautical miles, preserving space for domestic small-scale fleets. In October 2026 the Cabinet approved a nine-member board for the National Fishing Company, providing a formal state counterpart for joint ventures. The World Bank's US$50 million Badmaal project is concurrently financing landing-site infrastructure, community capacity and a national Fisheries Information Management System. Investment Priorities The most immediate opportunity is the cold chain. A value-chain study prepared for the World Bank found that, without integrated chilling, catches are routinely exposed to sea temperatures of 25–30°C, causing rapid spoilage, lost value and, in tuna, histamine-related food-safety risks (Matis). Ice plants, solar-powered cold rooms and insulated transport therefore offer a comparatively low-risk entry with immediate returns. Processing and export certification form the logical next step. Tuna canning, frozen lobster and dried products can serve Gulf and East African markets in the near term, while access to European markets will require an accredited competent authority and sanitary controls—an investment that early entrants should anticipate. Domestic semi-industrial fleets of 15–24-metre longliners and multipurpose vessels, financed by diaspora equity, represent a further opportunity, as do jetties, fish markets and auction halls at ports such as Mogadishu, Kismayo, Hobyo, Eyl and Bosaso, often co-financed through Badmaal. Finally, the Juba and Shabelle rivers and more than 10,000 square kilometers of inland water offer scope for aquaculture, while coastal sites suit seaweed and sea-cucumber farming (SATG). Energy: From Diesel Dependence to Renewable Opportunity Somalia's electricity sector presents a striking paradox. Consumers paid an average of approximately US$0.61 per kilowatt-hour in 2023—and more than US$1 in some areas served by private diesel generators—while more than 80 percent of generation still relies on imported diesel (Ecofin Agency, citing the World Bank). Yet the country receives average solar irradiance above 6 kWh per square meter per day and annual mean wind speeds exceeding 8 meters per second across most regions (Ministry of Energy and Water Resources), endowments that rank among the strongest in Africa. Installed solar capacity stood at only about 51 MW at the end of 2023 (PV magazine), and roughly half the population has access to electricity, falling to around 31 percent in rural areas. The government has set a target of 50 percent renewable electricity by 2028. The gap between today's diesel-based costs and the cost of new solar-plus storage capacity constitutes the core of the investment case. Market Structure and Regulation Somalia has no national grid. Electricity is supplied by private electricity service providers (ESPs) operating city-level networks and mini-grids, the largest being BECO in Mogadishu. This structure is unusual: the counterparties for new generation are private companies, and the sector already operates on private capital. The Electricity Act of 2023 established the National Electricity Authority (NEA) as the federal regulator, separating regulation from the policy role of the Ministry of Energy and Water Resources. NEA is now putting in place the regulatory architecture that investors require. This includes interim licensing instruments for generation and distribution developed with World Bank support; cost-of-service tariff regulation designed to align ESP tariffs with efficient costs and to reflect donor-financed assets; a national framework for independent power producers (IPPs) and standardized power purchase agreements (PPAs), supported under the EU-funded SDIT/GEED program; and draft Somali National Electrical Installation Guidelines, currently under stakeholder consultation. Program and Pipeline Development finance is building a substantial pipeline. The World Bank's US$100 million ASCENT Somalia project, running to 2028, seeks to expand access to clean energy through private-sector participation. Its flagship is a 45 MW solar photovoltaic plant with 140 MWh of battery storage at the Jazeera power station in Mogadishu, to be connected to BECO's network (Taiyang News). The Somali Electricity Sector Recovery Project is financing sector institutions, hybrid plants and the solarization of public facilities, including 585 public institutions (education and health facilities). The African Development Bank approved US$23 million in 2023 for solar generation and network upgrades in Bosaso, and the World Bank is preparing support for a first 500 kV transmission line that would begin to link Somalia's fragmented regional systems (ITSF). Opportunities for Investors For international and regional IPPs, the principal opportunity lies in grid-scale solar-plus-storage and wind plants selling power to ESPs under PPAs, once the national IPP/PPA framework and licenses are in force; coastal wind near Hobyo, Bosaso and Kismayo remain largely untapped. Domestic ESPs and investors can hybridize existing diesel networks, consolidate and upgrade city utilities, and extend distribution under regulated tariffs. Distributed energy town mini-grids, commercial and industrial rooftop solar, and productive-use systems such as solar irrigation pumps and cold rooms links the energy sector directly to agriculture and fisheries. Clean cooking and liquefied petroleum gas offer a further market, given the continued dominance of charcoal in household energy use. Agriculture and Livestock: Building on a Billion-Dollar Export Base Agriculture in its broadest sense crops, livestock and fisheries accounts for approximately 72 percent of Somalia's GDP (Ministry of Agriculture and Irrigation). The sector combines one of the country's great commercial successes, the livestock trade, with one of its largest untapped assets: irrigable land along the Juba and Shabelle rivers. Livestock Somalia's national herd is estimated at 56 to 57 million animals, supporting exports of between four and six million head a year, predominantly sheep and goats destined for Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Oman and Qatar (Dawan Africa). Central Bank data show export earnings rising from US$311 million in 2018 to approximately US$970 million in 2024, with 2025 projected to exceed US$1 billion for the first time (Food Business MEA). Market conditions have moved in Somalia's favor, conflict in Sudan and Australia's planned phase-out of live sheep exports by sea by 2028 have reduced competition in Gulf markets. The strategic opportunity is to move from exporting live animals to exporting value-added products. Export-certified abattoirs and chilled-meat facilities, feedlots and commercial fodder production, veterinary and quarantine services, hides and skins processing, and camel milk and dairy enterprises would each capture margins currently earned outside the country. Crops and Irrigation Of roughly 700,000 hectares suitable for pump or flood-recession irrigation, only about 110,800 hectares are currently irrigated less than half the area irrigated before the civil war (SOMINVEST). Somalia is nonetheless a significant global producer of sesame, grown principally in Lower Juba and Middle Shabelle. Under the FAO Hand-in-Hand Initiative, the government has presented an US$82.1 million investment case to raise sesame output by 50 percent, from 50,000 tons, alongside cases for maize, dairy and fodder (FAO). The European Union and Sweden are financing the rehabilitation of some 350 kilometers of irrigation canals on the two rivers (European Commission). These developments open several avenues for investors. Sesame hulling, oil extraction and tahini production would add value to a crop currently exported largely unprocessed, for which demand from China and the East African Community is strong. Commercial banana, lime and horticulture farms potentially organized throughout-grower schemes—could revive what was once a significant export trade. Irrigation services and solar-powered pumping address the gap between irrigated and irrigable land, while post-harvest storage, cold chains and phytosanitary laboratories are prerequisites for meeting export standards. Frankincense and myrrh from the north-east offer a high-value niche, and agricultural finance and insurance remain underdeveloped for smallholders who typically farm between 0.2 and 3 hectares. Domestic and Foreign Investors: Complementary Roles Somalia's largest pool of investable capital is domestic in origin. Central Bank data show total inward transfers reaching a record US$6.78 billion in 2025, of which individual remittances accounted for US$3.13 billion, or roughly 24 percent of GDP (The EastAfrican, citing the Central Bank of Somalia). Redirecting even a modest share of these flows from consumption into long-term productive equity would rival annual foreign direct investment. Different categories of investors bring distinct strengths. Domestic firms and business groups contribute local knowledge, established networks and existing operations in electricity supply, trade and telecommunications, and are well placed to lead mini-grid expansion, cold-chain development, fish markets and agro-processing. Diaspora investors combine hard-currency capital with international skills and a higher tolerance for local risk; commercial farms, fishing vessels, processing plants, hospitality and commercial solar suit their profile, and the National Diaspora Policy ratified in 2023 provides a framework for deeper engagement. Gulf and Turkish strategic investors, with established trade ties and existing port and logistics operations, are natural partners for ports, free zones, meat processing, large-scale agriculture and upstream energy, supported by bilateral investment treaties with Turkey, Germany and Egypt. International IPPs and specialist operators bring technology and project-finance experience for grid-scale renewables, tuna processing and certified abattoirs. Development finance institutions including the IDA Private Sector Window, the African Development Bank, IFC and EU blending facilities provide the concessional and risk-sharing capital that first-of-kind projects require. The Baidoa hybrid solar project demonstrates how these roles can be combined. In January 2023 MIGA issued its first guarantee in Somalia US$5.67 million for up to 15 years covering Kube Energy's investment in a plant that supplies the United Nations mission under a power purchase agreement (MIGA). A creditworthy offtake, political-risk cover and a first-loss layer from the IDA Private Sector Window together made the project bankable. The
